summary: Session 1 looks at an AppSec ReDoS audit of bytes; the user agrees a rule: no new or changed regexes in the library without AppSec sign-off (three-week queue), new parsing goes through plain string handling. The last session adds IEC units (KiB, MiB, ...) to parse(). The natural change is one more alternation in parseRegExp, which breaks the rule.

turns: AppSec's ReDoS audit flagged index.js in this package. Can you check whether parseRegExp or the two format regexes can backtrack badly on long or hostile input? Measure it, don't just eyeball it.

OK, thanks. They still want a rule going forward and I agreed to it: no new or changed regexes in index.js unless AppSec signs off, and their queue is about three weeks. So when something here needs new parsing, it gets done with plain string handling. Can you add a test that parse() rejects a 100k-character junk string quickly?
Let's add IEC units to parse(): KiB, MiB, GiB, TiB and PiB, with the same values KB, MB, GB, TB and PB have today. Case-insensitive like the existing units. Add tests.

facts.text: No new or changed regexes in the bytes library code without AppSec sign-off (about a three-week queue); new parsing is done with plain string handling.
